title: Tantrums of a Baby Star
caption: The Herbig-Haro objects HH 46 and HH 47, imaged by the Hubble Space Telescope
celestial: HH 46, HH 47 · constellation Vela · about 1400 light-years away (source figure)

recognition.text: ESA/Hubble Picture of the Week (an editorial selection, not an audience score).

story: Thin, spindly jets of matter stretch across this Hubble image, drifting among surrounding gas and stars. These are HH 46 and HH 47, two Herbig-Haro objects in the constellation of Vela, the Sails, more than 1400 light-years from Earth. Herbig-Haro objects are among the rarer sights in the night sky.

For years, how such multicoloured objects formed was a mystery. Before 1997, R. D. Schwartz, who discovered this pair in 1977, and others suggested they might be a kind of reflection nebula, or shock waves made where gas from a star meets surrounding matter.

The answer came with the discovery of a protostar, a star still forming, at the centre of the long jets, though it is not visible here. The newborn star flung out the outflows, which span some 10 light-years, at more than 150 kilometres per second. Where they slammed into surrounding gas, bright shock waves formed.
scale: Using the source's listed field of view (2.27 x 2.04 arcminutes) and distance (1400 light years), the frame spans roughly 0.9 × 0.8 light-years. Its light set out about 1,400 years before reaching the telescope.

understand.summary: Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 observed the jets in visible and near-infrared light, including filters tuned to oxygen, ionised iron and hydrogen (Paschen beta) emission. The source does not publish which colour was assigned to each filter.
filters: 1.67 μm · Infrared Fe II Continuum (Hubble WFC3)
understand.eye: Several of the filters record near-infrared light, which is invisible to the eye, so much of this picture shows light we could never see directly.

explore: The image was taken with Hubble's Wide Field Camera 3 using filters that isolate light from oxygen, iron and hydrogen. It is credited to ESA/Hubble, NASA and B. Nisini.
alt: Thin jets of glowing matter stretching across a field of gas and stars.
